title.narrative: Addressing urgent food needs in ISIS cleared and former Taliban held districts of Nangarhar

description.narrative: Late 2020, the Humanitarian situation in Afghanistan rapidly declined. High levels of violence and conflict, natural disasters, high rates of poverty, and the COVID-19 pandemic, contributed to a worsening humanitarian and grave protection crisis, causing significant displacement and high multi-sector humanitarian needs across the country. The armed conflict, ongoing for more than 40 years, was exhausting coping mechanisms of the population, making them extremely vulnerable. At the start of 2021, according to HRP Afghanistan 2021, 18.4 million people (nearly half the population) are in need of humanitarian assistance and 17.6 million Afghans are acute food insecure1. 50% of the children under 5 years are acute malnourished (HRP). The already precarious humanitarian situation was aggravated by the US/NATO Troops withdrawal announced earlier in 2021, but confirmed by the Biden Administration in April 2021. The US/ NATO Troops withdrawal intensified the conflict between the Afghan government and Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG) with fighting and displacement affecting nearly all provinces by July, causing loss of lives, further destruction and displacement by a rapidly advancing Taliban. From April until August, more than 670,000 people were displaced due to heavy fighting in the North (Kunduz), East (Nangarhar, Laghman) and South (Helmand & Kandahar) of the country. People were unable to tend to their fields and couldn’t harvest their crops, increasing food insecurity levels. Much to everybody’s surprise, the fighting came to an end on 15th August, when the former president of Afghanistan handed over Kabul peacefully to the Taliban to prevent further bloodshed. Recently the UN launched a new flash appeal, requesting an additional US$193M to cover the most urgent needs of 10 M Afghans until the end of the year, an increase of 2 M people. Additionally, in spring the previous government announced another drought2, likely to last 2 years and affecting food insecurity and food prices further. With most of the Afghans relying on agriculture, this is affecting their crops but also their income and live-stock, compounding the acute food insecurity.

Provision of cash for food to 4,820 extremely vulnerable conflict affected people in IPC 3 or IPC 4. Selected beneficiaries will receive half food basket cash for food for 2 months based on FSAC standards (Euro 150 in local currency) in one instalment.
To contribute to improved food security of conflict affected people in Afghanistan.

description.narrative: Appropriateness is assessed according to the SPHERE standards. A response is considered to be appropriate based on needs assessment, taking account of rights, needs, culture, age, gender, disabilities and context, and equity (non-discrimination and equal access.

Number of people who benefitted directly or indirectly from humanitarian assistance and/or resilient recovery services and/or disaster preparedness from activities in a humanitarian response implemented by Cordaid and implementing partners.

SPHERE: Communities and people affected by crisis, including the most vulnerable groups, consider that the timing of the assistance and protection they receive is adequate. DRA: timely depends on the nature of the acute crisis (slow versus sudden onset). If it is an acute sudden onset crisis a response is considered timely if we decide to respond within 48 hours and if we initiate the response within 72 hours. If it is a slow onset crisis, it is timely if we initiate the response in 3 weeks after we decide that the crisis meets the criteria of an acute crisis.
The applicable definition depends on the type of crisis (protracted versus acute). The SPHERE definition should be used in more protracted crisis where there is (more) time to conduct assessments and measure satisfaction of the response in the eyes of people affected. The DRA definition should be used for acute crises, where it is more important to initiate the response as soon as possible and look at our own processes.
